## 0. Frame
**System.** `coding-hermes-director` is a harness that runs a hierarchy of Hermes agents — one **director**, several **managers**, several **supervisors** — layered *above* the existing foremen/workers of the coding-hermes fleet, as a first-class system inside/alongside Hermes.
**One idea.** The hierarchy is *config the harness holds*, spoken through *chat rooms in DuckBrain*, timed by *the existing scheduler*: the harness registers ordinary scheduler triggers and answers when they fire; it never owns a schedule, never spawns directly, and never reconstructs a conversation — a message reaches an agent only as a brand-new session's first turn or an existing session's next turn, and every cycle ends in a report the harness verifies before more work is admitted.
**Why this exists (the waste it must kill).** The fleet already demonstrated the failure class this spec must make impossible: a foreman lane ran 213 dry-run ticks and burned 346M tokens in 48h (`FACT-22`, told-by-operator) because `admission_mode="tasks"` admits on workable rows alone (`FACT-01`, `FACT-02`) and the sanctions that exist (adaptive cooldown, dry-run throttle) were disabled or unreachable (`FACT-05`). A three-level hierarchy of chatting agents multiplies that failure surface by every edge in the org chart. The director harness must be built so a fully-deferred fleet *idles* rather than *converses*.
**Readers.** (a) The **owner** decides the quorum items in §7; (b) a **worker/foreman** must be able to build one milestone (§8) from this file plus the cited source without inventing a contract; (c) a **judge** must be able to grade every acceptance criterion in §8 as run/pass/fail.
**Scope boundary (explicit).** This spec does NOT cover: changing foreman or worker prompts (they are untouched); the scheduler's packer/admission algorithms (reused, not modified, except where §3.5 names an extension); DuckBrain internals (used over its HTTP API only — the chat system of §4.4 is *defined* as DuckBrain key families, not a fork of DuckBrain); Muster internals (borrowed, at most, for MCP tool exposure — `OQ-4`). Cross-fleet director-to-director federation is OUT of scope for the v2 build; it is recorded as a future extension, note only (§4.7).

### 1.2 Known unknowns (articulated, unverified — register §A.2)
The highest-value unknowns, each with a probe and a falsifier:
- **UQ-1 (blocking, M2).** Does a Hermes gateway session *continue conversation context* when a second prompt is sent with the same `session_key` (`FACT-11` shows the scheduler already transmits one)? This decides how strong REUSE mode (§4.1) is: full conversation continuation vs a delivered message with no memory of prior turns. Probe: two gateway POSTs, same key, second asks "what did I just say". Falsifier: second answer shows no memory of the first prompt → REUSE mode is attribution-only; multi-turn context then lives in the ROOM LOG, which agents read themselves (§4.4) — never harness-reconstructed. The verify-loop re-prompt (§5.1) is self-contained either way. - **UQ-2 (blocking for §6.2 backstop).** DuckBrain read API shape (`GET`/query endpoints) and whether tokens can be *namespace-scoped* (a token valid for one namespace only). Probe: read the DuckBrain route table; mint a scoped token and try a cross-namespace read. Falsifier: if scoping does not exist, read-scoping (§6.2) must be enforced **entirely** at the harness router, and DuckBrain tokens stay host-trusted. - **UQ-3 (non-blocking, M3).** Whether `POST /projects/{name}/bump` (`FACT-14`) can express "admit once at time T" or only "raise admission frequency for N ticks". Determines how scheduled wakes request admission (§3.3). Falsifier: bump body fields admit only `remaining_ticks`-style knobs → propose the `wake_once` extension in §3.5 as a scheduler PR. - **UQ-4 (non-blocking).** Muster's MCP surface shape (what a tool exposed via Muster looks like to a Hermes session). Told-by-operator only (`FACT-24`). Falsifier: Muster cannot expose per-namespace tools → role tool grants (§6.1) fall back to Hermes config profiles alone. - **UQ-5 (non-blocking).** The exact Hermes knob for per-session tool restriction (config profiles vs CLI flags on `hermes chat`). Falsifier: no per-session restriction exists → tool grants degrade to harness-side sandboxing and the §6.1 matrix marks those rows UNVERIFIED. - **UQ-6 (non-blocking, M5).** DuckBrain's search surface over room keys (full-text? prefix only?) — decides how much of "searchable chat log" (§4.4) DuckBrain provides vs what the harness indexes. Probe: read the DuckBrain API docs; try a query endpoint. Falsifier: no server-side search → the harness keeps a lightweight inverted index over room keys and DuckBrain remains the durable store only. - **UQ-7 (non-blocking, M3).** DuckBrain room-write atomicity: do two agents appending to the same room concurrently always get distinct, monotonic `<seq>` values (server-allocated), or can they race? Probe: concurrent POSTs to one key family; read back the sequence. Falsifier: client-chosen seq can collide → the harness allocates seq through a single writer (its own API) and agents POST through it.

### 1.3 Unknown unknowns (techniques named; each lands as a risk or a design decision)
- **Assumption inversion** on K10 ("sessions are fire-and-forget"): if a re-prompt *does* continue a session (REUSE mode, §4.1), a stuck session keeps its whole conversation on every remind — including the confusion that made it stall. Design consequence: the fresh-session rung of the ladder (§5.1) is *mandatory*, not optional, even when REUSE re-prompts "work". - **Cross-domain analogy** (Kubernetes operator / Airflow scheduler): a hierarchy where leaves schedule themselves degenerates into thundering-herd; the fix everywhere else is *one owner of the queue and workload, centralized admission*. Imported as D-002 (§3.1) — in v2 the existing scheduler IS that single admission authority and the harness adds no second one (RL-1). - **Scale extremes** at 100× (100 agents chatting): naive agent-to-agent messaging is O(n²) sessions. Room-based messaging (§4.2–§4.4) and per-gateway concurrency limits (§3.4) exist precisely for this; the design caps fan-out at `orchestration.max_fanout` (default 12, matching the foreman wave budget in `FACT-16`'s default_prompt). - **Second-order effects** (success case): if the director works, foremen get *better* task selection — which hides the director's own failures ("fleet looks fine, hierarchy does nothing"). Consequence: §8 milestones require the harness's own observability (send ledger, outcome counters), not just fleet health. - **Day-one state**: before the first trigger is registered, the harness must show zero agents woken, zero rooms, zero sends — and the fleet must run exactly as today. Normative: **the director harness is additive; with an empty config it is a no-op** (R-012). - **Unexpressible failure**: if a session cannot record "I failed" (no report message posted), every downstream count lies. Consequence: the report contract (§4.5) defines an explicit `failed` status, and "no report at deadline" is a *distinct, countable* state (§5.1). - **Adversary view**: an agent that benefits from appearing productive. It posts a report claiming `done` with no artifact. Consequence: report verification (§4.5) requires an artifact reference for `done`, and the harness samples artifact existence (M5 criterion).

### 1.4 Unknown knowns (operator-held constraints, made explicit)
- **N-1.** The scheduler's own law: *nothing added to the system may veto, skip, or delay a spawn* — the G1/G7 ruling quoted at `internal/scheduler/board_wake.go:34-38` (`FACT-13`). The director inherits this law: **the hierarchy orders and requests; it never overrides admission** (R-003). - **N-2.** Both stores must agree on every write: scheduler changes land in `~/.hermes/coding-hermes/scheduler.db` **and** `~/.hermes/fleet.toml` (told-by-operator, `FACT-26`; pin-import mechanics at `FACT-07`). Any director config that adds lanes must go through the pinned loader/API path, never by editing the DB directly (R-014). - **N-3.** "Fast when there is work, slow when it is only perpetual stuff" — the owner's stated intent for tasks mode (quoted at `internal/scheduler/admission_mode.go:44-46`). The director adopts the same doctrine for its own wakes (R-013). - **N-4.** Stated non-goal inherited from fleet history: the director must NOT re-introduce retired driver scripts or custom `command` lanes (`FACT-09` exists because that class of config rotted).

### 2.2 Component contracts
Each contract states what a caller may rely on and what the producer may not break. Producer/consumer both named.
**CT-01 — Config registry (harness-owned; RL-2).** Producer: the operator (and, in M1, the config loader). Consumers: every harness component. Content: `[[gateways]]` (id, url, transport, `auth_token_ref`, `max_inflight`) and `[[agents]]` (id, role, `gateway` binding, `skills` list, `responsibility`, session bonding, room membership, triggers). The harness is the ONLY owner of this mapping: no agent may edit its own binding, skills, or membership (§6.3). The harness provisions skill lists INTO the named gateways and derives everything scheduler-side from this one file (R-001).
**CT-02 — Trigger registration → scheduler (RL-1).** Producer: the harness. Consumer: the existing scheduler. The harness registers NORMAL scheduler lanes/triggers (cooldown mode, validated config path `FACT-07`/`FACT-08`, two-store agreement `N-2`) for the director and, individually, for any manager needing its own clock. Each trigger lane's per-lane `gateway_url` names the harness API (`FACT-27`) — so when the trigger fires, the scheduler POSTs the tick to the harness. Idempotent on `dedupe_key`. The harness owns NO wake table of its own (supersedes v1 §3.3; OQ-6 superseded in §A.2).
**CT-03 — Harness → scheduler (admission request).** On a fire callback, the harness calls itself back into its cycle path and requests admission through the scheduler's existing public surface — the bump API `POST /api/v1/projects/{name}/bump` (`FACT-14`) or, if UQ-3 resolves to "extension needed", the small `wake_once` extension of §3.5. **The harness never spawns directly**; the scheduler remains the sole admission authority (`FACT-13`, R-003, R-018). Backpressure: the orchestrator respects per-gateway `max_inflight` (§3.4, RL-7) and the namespace `max_concurrent` it configured (`FACT-16`); the scheduler may admit less.
**CT-04 — Scheduler → gateway → session (the only two delivery modes; RL-3).** Unchanged transport: gateway POST with prompt, model, provider, and `session_key` (`FACT-11`). The harness adds exactly one decision — the session mode: - **NEW**: a brand-new session (fresh session key); the message is its first turn. - **REUSE**: the agent's existing bonded session (same session key); the message is its next turn. There is no third mode. The harness NEVER reconstructs conversation history into the prompt (no "last N messages", no `CONVERSATION SO FAR` — v1 §4.1/§4.3 are deleted). Context lives in the room log, which agents read themselves (§4.4). Auth rejection is terminal (`FACT-12`).
**CT-05 — Session → DuckBrain (room writes + reports).** Every hierarchy session, on every wake, posts zero or more chat messages to rooms it is a member of and exactly one report message (§4.5), authenticated with its role token (`FACT-19`, `FACT-20`). Key layout in §4.4. The session has no other write surface for these key families. Room-append sequencing is race-safe by UQ-7's outcome.
**CT-06 — Verify loop.** Consumer of CT-05. `Verify(send_id, agent_id) → verified | no_report | bad_report | failed`. `verified` requires a FRESH report (RL-20): the loop machine-checks `report.timestamp > request.timestamp` — an attached older report does not satisfy the loop and is `bad_report{reason: stale}`. On `no_report`/`bad_report`, runs the ladder of §5.1, expressed in the only two session modes: remind = a REUSE-mode message into the bonded session (up to N=2; `FACT-11` makes the key plumb-through possible; UQ-1 decides how much context survives), then one **NEW session**, then **escalate** into the parent's room and, at the top, to the owner. The NEW-session rung needs no history restore: the prompt states the obligation, and the agent reads the room for context.
**CT-07 — Chat Router (membership + wake routing).** Producer: sessions (via DuckBrain writes). Consumer: the router. When a message lands in a room (including a `kind=report` message), the router resolves membership and computes which agent sessions to wake — exact target for a person-directed reply or `@handle`, all other members for a group-directed one — subject to per-gateway limits (§3.4). **The router is the only component that resolves room membership**; sessions are told their own rooms and never learn another room's keys (§6.2 for the enforcement point).
**CT-08 — Scheduling ownership rule.** Agents never schedule themselves (R-021). An agent may REQUEST a future wake ("do this in 2 hours") by asking the harness; the harness registers it as a normal scheduler trigger (CT-02) and, when it fires, the wake comes back as a chat message into the agent's room/session. An agent self-scheduling outside that path is a violation counted as a bad report (§4.5).
**CT-09 — Responsibilities registry (RL-8).** The config's `responsibility` field per agent is the authoritative registry; the harness mirrors it to DuckBrain keys (`registry/<agent-id>`, §4.4) so any agent (and any human reader) can resolve "who owns X" without reading the harness config. Manager-to-manager rooms (`kind: space`) are config data whose membership SHOULD be justified by the registry; the router refuses to deliver into a space whose members do not both carry a registry entry (M5 acceptance).
**CT-10 — VP caller role (RL-13).** Producer: VP callers. Consumer: the harness ingress (CT-14). A VP is any of the owner's own agent surfaces — Hermes (which has a TOOL to call the director), Claude Code, anything that speaks MCP or calls the harness API correctly. A VP talks to the director AS a first-class caller: it sends messages and chats just like a manager does. VP grants, exactly three: create objectives (open rooms), inject messages into rooms it names, read rooms it names. **Harness-internal agents (managers, supervisors, the director's own sessions) can NOT act as VP unless explicitly granted** — default-deny, one §6.1 table row, one config grant per agent. Every VP signal leaves the same audit record regardless of which door it entered.
**CT-11 — Missing-reply handling (RL-11).** Producer: the harness verify loop. Consumers: the caller agent and the target agent. When a message is sent agent→agent, the reply might never come; failure is detectable MECHANICALLY — the target agent neither posted a reply message nor came back with an attached work report. On detection the harness does BOTH: (a) notifies the CALLER (the agent above) that their reply never arrived, and (b) sends a BUMP to the session that was supposed to be producing the report. This is an extension of the existing remind→fresh→escalate ladder (§5.1) — it rides those rungs, it does not fork a second mechanism.
**CT-12 — Threaded replies (RL-12).** Producer: every replying session. Consumer: the chat router. A reply is a message IN A SUBTHREAD of the original request: each message carries `reply_to` (its parent seq); the original request is the ROOT; one branch per task; nesting is unbounded (a reply to a reply is itself replyable). Multiple supervisors — or a supervisor and its manager — working ONE task share the SAME subthread. The thread is data over the room's single DuckBrain log (walk `reply_to` over `chd/room/<room-id>/<seq>`), never a second store; wake targeting is unchanged (§4.4).
**CT-13 — Per-agent instance limits + typed caps; DuckBrain is the only store (RL-14, RL-15).** Producer: the send orchestrator. Consumers: every dispatch. Two INDEPENDENT limits: (1) per-agent `max_sessions` — the max concurrent LIVE sessions of one agent id, because the same agent can run multiple sessions at once — separate from and never derived from (2) per-gateway `max_inflight`. The service config also carries the typed caps: max concurrent agents on a Hermes gateway AND max concurrent agents of a given TYPE in parallel. **Scheduling is always allowed; RUNNING is what the cap gates** — a wake is scheduled and queued, not refused, when a cap is full. All durable state — every room, message, report, session bond, registry entry, and limit — is stored in DuckBrain (key families §4.5); there is no second durable store.
**CT-14 — Signal ingress: one surface, four doors (RL-16).** Producer: the harness. Consumers: VPs, the scheduler acting as VP, and the owner's UI chat (§11.3). The harness drives Hermes harnesses via signals arriving at exactly four ingress points — API, MCP, CLI, webhook (§11.2) — enumerated as ONE contract surface: same authentication, same VP-signal semantics, same audit record, no door privileged. The scheduler's tick fire (CT-02) is a signal on the same surface, with the scheduler acting as VP.
**CT-15 — Crier bridge (RL-18).** Producer: the bridge adapter. Consumer: the crier fleet bus (`~/crier`, FACT-32). A bridge adapter so director rooms/events can reach crier and vice versa: outbound, a configured room event is published to a crier topic or delivered to a crier agent's durable inbox; inbound, a retrieved crier message becomes a room message posted through the harness ingress (CT-14), passing the same auth and audit as any VP message. No hierarchy contract (verify loop, ladder, caps) reads or writes crier; a crier outage degrades the bridge only (§11.4).

## 3. Scheduling: Scheduler Callback, No New Engine

### 3.1 Decision D-001/D-002: config-holding harness on the existing scheduler
**D-001 (revised for RL-1).** The harness is a **config holder + callback service on the EXISTING scheduler** — not a second scheduling engine. The scheduler already owns everything the hierarchy must not re-implement: admission (`admission_mode.go`), concurrency slots (`slot_pool.go:27,90-91`, `FACT-10`), cooldown pins with DB authority (`loader.go:881-893`, `FACT-07`), budget caps, blackout windows (`FACT-17`), gateway spawn with error classification (`FACT-11`, `FACT-12`), and a fail-closed mutation gate (`FACT-15`). v1's harness-owned `wake_schedule` table is DELETED: the wake schedule is the scheduler's own trigger rows (CT-02), keeping ONE admission authority (R-018).
**D-002.** Agents never self-schedule. All wakes are admitted by the existing scheduler. The harness's role is narrower than v1's: hold the config (RL-2), register triggers, answer fire callbacks, enforce per-gateway concurrency, and verify reports. This is the same shape the scheduler itself chose for board wakes — "the watcher only ADDS evaluation triggers" (`FACT-13`) — applied one level up.

### 3.2 The harness config: gateways, skills, responsibilities (RL-2, RL-7, RL-8)
One file, `harness.toml`, operator-owned (R-001). The full schema mirror lives in the skill's `fleet-config-schema.yaml` (schema_version 2);
```toml # harness.toml — the ONE hierarchy config. The harness derives from it: # scheduler trigger lanes (§3.3), gateway skill injection, room # provisioning, and the DuckBrain responsibilities registry.
[[gateways]] id = "gw-main" url = "http://127.0.0.1:8642" transport = "loopback" # loopback | tailscale | ssh-tunnel | direct (§9) max_inflight = 4 # per-gateway concurrency limit (§3.4, RL-7)
[[gateways]] id = "gw-bunker" url = "http://bunker-host.tailnet:8642" transport = "tailscale" auth_token_ref = "bunker-gw" max_inflight = 2
[[agents]] id = "mgr-infra" role = "manager" gateway = "gw-main" # BINDING: this manager runs on this gateway skills = ["coding-hermes-manager", "coding-hermes-foreman"] # injected by the harness (RL-2) responsibility = "infra: crier, lore, bunker foreman lanes" # registry entry (RL-8) session = { bond = "objective", reuse_policy = "reuse-until-wedged" } triggers = ["0 */6 * * *"] # registered as scheduler trigger lanes (§3.3) rooms = ["obj-infra", "space-infra-ops"] # memberships (config data, never discovered)
[[agents]] id = "sup-crier" role = "supervisor" gateway = "gw-main" skills = ["coding-hermes-supervisor-subagent-base"] responsibility = "crier lane data-gathering and bounded actions" session = { bond = "task" } triggers = [] # supervisors are woken by messages, not clocks rooms = ["task-crier-*"] ```
Field semantics the rest of the spec relies on:
- `gateway` — the binding (RL-2, RL-7): every agent runs on exactly one named gateway; §9's multi-host endpoint fields (`transport`, `auth_token_ref`) live on the gateway row, so host routing and concurrency are decided in ONE place. - `skills` — the role's skill list (RL-2). The harness writes these into the named gateway's session configuration and re-writes them on config change; agents never edit their own skill list. - `responsibility` — the registry entry (RL-8), mirrored by the harness to DuckBrain `chd/registry/<agent-id>` so the org chart is readable by agents and humans alike. - `session` — bonding (RL-4): `bond` names what the session is attached to (an objective room, a task room, or the agent's own work); `reuse_policy` selects between the two delivery modes of CT-04 and is the only knob that can override REUSE (→ NEW) for a wedged session.

### 3.3 Trigger registration and the fire round trip (RL-1)
**Two hops, always (RL-10, R-023).** The call path is now CONFIRMED and normative: the scheduler calls the director-harness, and the director-harness calls the gateway. Two hops, every dispatch — the scheduler never spawns a hierarchy agent directly, and the harness never reaches an agent except through its gateway.
1. **Registration.** At startup (and on config change), the harness registers one scheduler trigger lane per configured clock: the director's sync lane and any per-manager lanes. Each is a NORMAL cooldown-mode lane in the `director` namespace, landed through the validated config path (`FACT-08`, `FACT-07`, two-store agreement `N-2`). Its per-lane `gateway_url` names the harness API (`FACT-27`, `FACT-28`); its payload names the callback (`cycle=director-sync` or `cycle=manager-<id>`). 2. **Fire.** The scheduler's cooldown clock admits the trigger lane and POSTs the tick to the harness API — the trigger calls the main system. 3. **Call-back.** The harness receives the fire and calls itself back into its cycle path: compose sends (§3.4), request admission for woken agents via bump (`FACT-14`), and return 2xx to the scheduler so the trigger tick completes cleanly. The scheduler logs the trigger tick like any other; the harness's own ledger records what the cycle did.
If UQ-3 resolves to "bump cannot express admit-once", the `wake_once` extension (§3.5) replaces step 3's admission request — the round trip itself does not change.

### 3.4 Backpressure IS per-gateway concurrency (RL-7)
- **The limit is per gateway.** Each `[[gateways]]` row carries `max_inflight` — the number of concurrent agent requests that gateway may run. Managers are BOUND to a gateway (§3.2), so the director waking thirty managers fans out across gateways, never into one. - **The limit is ALSO per agent (RL-14).** The same agent id can run MULTIPLE sessions at once, so each `[[agents]]` row carries its own `max_sessions` — the max concurrent LIVE sessions of that one agent id — separate from, and never derived from, the gateway's `max_inflight`. A gateway with headroom can still be at an agent's own cap; the orchestrator checks BOTH before dispatch (CT-13). - **Caps gate RUNNING, never scheduling (RL-15).** The service config carries the typed limits: max concurrent agents on a Hermes gateway, and max concurrent agents of a given TYPE in parallel. Scheduling is always allowed — a wake is composed and queued even when a cap is full; RUNNING is what the cap gates. A queued send is a scheduled agent waiting its turn, not a refused one. - **The harness enforces it.** Before sending to any agent, the orchestrator checks the target gateway's inflight count (its own counter, cross-checked with scheduler running-tick reads where available, OQ-10). At the limit, sends for that gateway QUEUE — nothing is dispatched. Queued sends age with exponential backoff on re-composition; a send older than `orchestration.stale_after` (default 2× cycle) is marked `deferred{reason: backpressure}`, counted, and dropped (the next scheduled cycle supersedes it — no unbounded queue). - **Event-driven responses.** An agent finishing its turn replies into the chat room (CT-05); the router sees the message and wakes the addressed agent(s) (CT-07) — subject to the same per-gateway limits. No agent polls; no agent schedules itself (R-021). A scheduled future wake ("do this in 2 hours") rides a registered scheduler trigger (CT-08) and arrives as a chat message. - **Scheduler-side authority is untouched.** Namespace `max_concurrent` and SlotPool caps apply regardless of what the harness requests (`FACT-10`, `FACT-16`); blackout windows still shift cost (`FACT-17`). The hierarchy is deliberately configured to *lose* to production lanes: director namespace weight low, `reserved=0`. - **Monitoring.** Every send has a row in a `send_log`: send_id, room, thread id (RL-12), target, session mode (NEW/REUSE), gateway, dispatch timestamps, verify outcome (CT-06), close reason. Counters: `sends_total`, `sends_deferred{reason}`, `reports_missing_total`, `missing_reply_total` (RL-11), `reprompts_total{rung}`, `gateway_inflight{gateway}`, `sessions_live{agent}` (RL-14). A send closes when its row reaches a terminal state or the deadline (`verify.deadline_s`, default 1800) expires.

### 3.5 Reuse vs extension of the scheduler daemon
**Reused unchanged:** admission, packer, SlotPool, cooldown pins, budgets, blackouts, gateway client, auth gate, board-freshness reading — and now ALSO the trigger surface itself (CT-02), which v1 proposed to duplicate.
**Ridden as-is if possible:** wave/send admission via the bump API (`POST /api/v1/projects/{name}/bump`, `FACT-14`). SPIKE (UQ-3): bump's body semantics (raise frequency vs admit-once) must be confirmed; the bump test asserts only the 200 contract.
**Extension (only if UQ-3 falsifies bump):** a `wake_once` admission request — either a bump body field or a small API route — meaning "make lane L eligible for exactly one admission at or before T; if not picked, expire". It must respect the scheduler's law: it may add an evaluation trigger, never force a spawn (`FACT-13`). Config must land through the loader's validated path (`FACT-08` mode validation; `FACT-07` pin authority), keeping the two-store agreement (`N-2`).
**Why not a harness-side cron calling `hermes chat` directly:** that is the worker-spawn pattern today (`FACT-23` — a foreman shells out to `hermes chat -q`). It works for one worker because the foreman is present to verify. A hierarchy with no one watching would repeat the dry-run failure class; the harness *is* the watcher — but a watcher that owns no clock (RL-1).
## 4. Objectives, Tasks, and the DuckBrain Chat System

### 4.1 Session model: owned sessions and the only two delivery modes (RL-3, RL-4)
Every agent — director, manager, supervisor — has its OWN session: its own system prompt, its own skills (injected per RL-2), its own work. Sessions are ordinary Hermes sessions; there is no resident process to message, and the harness NEVER composes a conversation out of stored messages (v1's history restore is deleted). When anything needs an agent to act, the harness delivers a message to that agent's session in one of exactly two modes:
- **REUSE** — send the message into the agent's existing bonded session (same `session_key`). `reuse_policy` in §3.2 governs when REUSE is retired in favor of NEW (default: reuse until the ladder of §5.1 declares the session wedged). - **NEW** — create a brand-new session and make the message its first turn.
Both modes use the controller dispatch path (CT-03, CT-04): a scheduled fire reaches the controller callback and the controller performs the shared reservation and gateway POST; an authorized immediate request reaches the same controller primitive without a scheduler lane. The scheduler is trigger/callback-only; the gateway spawns and Hermes records the `session_key` (`FACT-11`; resume semantics `FACT-29`). Whether REUSE carries full conversational context is UQ-1; the design works either way because durable context lives in the room log (§4.4), which agents read themselves — opening a room and reading is an agent tool action, not harness prompt-reconstruction.

### 4.2 OBJECTIVES are chat rooms (RL-4)
The DIRECTOR makes objectives. An objective is sent directly to a manager's gateway — or to a group of managers when the objective needs one — and an objective IS A CHAT ROOM:
- Backed by DuckBrain key families (§4.4): `chd/room/<objective-id>/<seq>`, one ordered, searchable log per objective. - Readable by a HUMAN like a Slack group: every agent message is a message — visible, ordered, attributed (`from`), searchable. No harness translation layer; the room is the artifact. - Membership: the director + one or more managers (config data, §3.2). The director's objective message is the room's first directive; manager replies, questions, and reports accumulate in the same log. - Each participant's OWN session is BONDED to the objective (`session.bond = "objective"`, §3.2): the objective is not a prompt the agent once received — it is the room the agent's session is attached to, and every wake lands as a message in that room.
**Future extension (note only, not in scope):** two directors, or cross-fleet director-to-director rooms with shared managers. Nothing in the room schema precludes it (a room's members are config data; a second director is another member), but no v2 milestone builds it, and the security model of §6 assumes exactly one director per namespace until the owner rules otherwise.

### 4.3 TASKS are chat rooms (RL-5)
MANAGERS make tasks — goals, stories; the word is flexible — and send them to supervisors in another DuckBrain chat room:
- `chd/room/task-<id>/<seq>`, members = the manager + its supervisors for that task (config data, §3.2). - The manager's task message is the room's opening post; supervisors do bounded work and reply into the room; each agent still has its own bonded session (`session.bond = "task"`). - A supervisor finishing replies INTO the chat (CT-05); that reply WAKES the manager (event-driven, RL-7) — subject to per-gateway limits (§3.4).

### 4.4 Chat semantics, baked into DuckBrain (RL-6, RL-8)
The chat system is DuckBrain key families — not a harness-internal invention. One ordered family per room, searchable:
- **Layout.** `chd/room/<room-id>/<seq>` — `<seq>` monotonic per room (writer: the sending session via its role token, `FACT-19`/`FACT-20`; race-safety per UQ-7). Threads are a TREE over the same family (RL-12, below); nothing is stored outside the room's single log. - **Message content** is JSON: `{from, to, room, seq, reply_to?, kind: msg|directive|task|report|incident, body, attach?: [report keys], ts}`. - **Threads are a tree (RL-12).** Replying to a message means replying IN A SUBTHREAD of the original request: a message may carry `reply_to: <seq>` (its parent), and the chain of `reply_to` links is the thread. The ROOT of a thread is the original request message; there is one branch per task; threads NEST ARBITRARILY — tag an agent, it replies, that reply is itself replyable, and the thread goes down as deep as needed. Multiple supervisors (or a supervisor and its manager) working ONE task share the SAME subthread: they all reply into the branch the task hangs from. The tree is read by walking `reply_to` over the room's single log — never a second store. - **Owner posting.** The human (owner) can post into any room (`from: owner`). The harness does NOT deliver the owner's own message back to the owner — no self-echo. The message is in the log; the owner reads it there like everyone else. - **Replies target a person or the group.** `to: "<agent-id>"` routes the wake to that one agent; `to: "group"` wakes all other members (subject to gateway limits). The log itself is indifferent — every message is visible to every member, targeting only decides who is WOKEN. - **@-handles (later).** `to: "@<agent-id>"` — an explicit single-agent wake; the message still lives in the room log for search regardless of whether the target is online. The @-wake feature may lag the build (flagged at M5); person-directed `to:` works from day one. - **Search.** Rooms are DuckBrain keys; any member (and any human with DuckBrain access) can search the log. UQ-6 probes how much search DuckBrain provides natively. - **Registry keys.** `chd/registry/<agent-id>` — the responsibilities registry mirrored by the harness (CT-09); a manager-to-manager room's membership is justified by these entries (RL-8). - **Manager-to-manager spaces.** Rooms of `kind: space` connect managers whose `responsibility` entries overlap (RL-8); they are config data, and the router refuses membership the registry does not justify (CT-09, M5).

### 4.5 The report contract (owed by every agent, every wake)
A finished task's report arrives AS a chat message with the report attached (RL-6): the agent posts `kind=report` into its room; the report JSON is the attachment. The receiving agent opens it or not — the log records both ways.
Namespace: `chd` (director namespace; DuckBrain supports namespaces — told-by-operator, consistent with per-project token files at `FACT-20`).
| Key | Writer | Content | |-----|--------|---------| | `chd/room/<room-id>/<seq>` | the agent | message JSON; `kind=report` carries the report object as its attachment; `reply_to` places it in its subthread (RL-12) | | `chd/registry/<agent-id>` | **harness only** | responsibilities registry mirror (CT-09) | | `chd/bond/<agent-id>` | **harness only** | the agent's SESSION BOND record — what its session is attached to (RL-15) | | `chd/limits/<scope>` | **harness only** | the effective typed caps mirrored from service config: per-gateway and per-type concurrent-agent limits, per-agent `max_sessions` (RL-14/RL-15) | | `chd/send/<send-id>/manifest` | **harness only** | send composition record (replaces v1's wave manifest) |
**All data in DuckBrain (RL-15).** Every room, message, report, session bond, registry entry, and limit is stored in DuckBrain — the families above are the complete set, and there is no second durable store. The service config is the AUTHORITY for the limits; the `chd/limits/<scope>` keys mirror them so agents and the UI (§11.3) read the effective caps without reading the config. A harness build that persists any of this anywhere else violates R-028.
**Fresh-report rule (RL-20).** A PREVIOUS report may be delivered as a message — an agent is free to point at an older report for context — but the reply contract still requires a FRESH report for the current request: the report must be NEWER than the request it answers. The verify loop machine-checks `report.timestamp > request.timestamp`; an attached old report does not satisfy the loop and is `bad_report{reason: stale}` (CT-06), which re-enters the ladder of §5.1.
Report JSON (validated by the verify loop; a report failing validation is `bad_report`):
```json { "send_id": "s-20261107-1530-a1b2", "agent": "sup-crier", "room": "task-crier-42", "status": "done | deferred | blocked | failed", "summary": "one paragraph, human-readable", "artifacts": ["board row id", "commit sha", "duckbrain key"], "next": "optional: what the next cycle should do", "ts": "2026-11-07T15:31:00Z" } ```
Rules: `status=done` requires ≥1 artifact reference; the harness samples artifact existence (M5). `deferred` requires a reason; a cycle whose every send defers closes as **drained** (§5.6). Custom report tables (e.g. a director-defined fleet-health table) are optional DuckBrain tables declared by the director; agents write rows only into tables named in their `grants` (§6.1).

### 4.6 Read scoping (survived from v1, re-pointed at rooms)
The v1 read-scoping guarantees survive unchanged in meaning, with "channel" → "room": an agent may read its OWN log and the logs of rooms it is a member of; never another pair's room, never a room it is not in. The enforcement point is §6.2 (router primary, token backstop). Room membership is config data (§3.2) plus the registry justification of CT-09 — never discovered by agents.

### 4.7 Future extension — cross-fleet (note only, RL-4)
Two directors, or director-to-director rooms across fleets with shared managers, are a natural extension of the room model (members are data). Explicitly NOT built in v2: no milestone, no security ruling, no config surface. Recorded so the room schema is not accidentally narrowed.

## 5. Failure Modes

### 5.1 Session never writes its report — the ladder
Deadline: `verify.deadline_s` (default 1800) after dispatch, well inside the gateway tick timeout (`FACT-21`). The ladder speaks only the two session modes of CT-04 — it never reconstructs history (RL-3).
1. **Rung 0 — remind (REUSE).** Post a remind message into the agent's bonded session ("your report for room `…` is missing; post it now"). Up to `N=2` times, spaced `verify.remind_gap_s` (default 300). Whether context persists across these prompts is UQ-1; the remind is self-contained either way. 2. **Rung 1 — fresh session (NEW).** One brand-new session; the prompt states the report obligation first and names the room. The agent reads the room itself for context (§4.4). Rationale: a fresh session escapes a wedged context, and per §1.3 this rung is mandatory even when rung 0 "worked". 3. **Rung 2 — escalate.** Mark the send `escalated`; post a `kind=incident` message to the agent's parent room. The director aggregates incidents; three incidents from the same agent in a rolling 24h is an owner-page (§7). 4. Every rung is counted (`reprompts_total{rung}`); the send row records which rung closed it. **No rung silently resets the counters.**
**Missing replies (RL-11, CT-11).** The ladder also covers the case where the REPLY to an agent→agent message never comes. Detection is mechanical: the target agent neither replied (no message in the subthread, RL-12) nor came back with an attached work report. On detection the harness does BOTH:
- (a) **notify the CALLER** — the agent above, whose message went unanswered — that their reply never arrived; and - (b) **send a BUMP to the session** that was supposed to be producing the report — a REUSE-mode message restating the fresh-report obligation (below), riding rung 0's cadence.
The bump then walks the SAME rungs: remind → fresh session → escalate. A missing reply that survives rung 1 becomes an escalated incident exactly like a missing report, counted as `missing_reply_total` (§3.4). This extends the ladder; it does not fork a second mechanism.
**Every rung demands a FRESH report (RL-20).** A re-prompt — remind or bump — restates the current request's obligation, and only a report newer than that request closes the loop (`report.timestamp > request.timestamp`, machine-checked); an attached older report re-enters the ladder as `bad_report{reason: stale}`.

### 5.2 A manager stops responding
Same ladder, rung 2 posts the incident to the **director's** room. If the manager accumulates `escalations >= 3` in 24h, the harness sets its dependents' sends to `deferred{reason: parent_down}` — children are not left self-scheduling — and pages the owner. Recovery is automatic on the manager's next verified report.

### 5.3 DuckBrain down
Health: the harness polls `/health` (`FACT-18`) with a 10s interval. **Write path down: sends do not dispatch at all** — a cycle whose reports cannot be persisted is a cycle whose verify loop cannot close, so dispatching it only manufactures unaccountable sessions. Queued sends back off exponentially and the send log records `duckbrain_unavailable`. No agent is woken into a black hole. (v1's degraded-empty-history read path is deleted with history reconstruction itself; with rooms as the context store, no store means no dispatch.)

### 5.4 Gateway down
The scheduler already classifies gateway failures: auth rejection is terminal, transport/5xx are transient with bounded retry and Retry-After honored (`FACT-11`, `FACT-12`). The harness adds nothing here; it observes sends stuck in `dispatched` past deadline and treats them per §5.1. A gateway-wide outage (multiple agents on one gateway failing the same cycle) surfaces through the scheduler's existing failure events; the harness pauses send composition to that gateway when the scheduler reports failure backoff on its lanes. Session resume after gateway drop or daemon restart is the scheduler's own SCHED-GAP-091 machinery (`FACT-29`) — resumed sessions continue under REUSE semantics.

### 5.5 Load gates — per-gateway concurrency is the mechanism (RL-7)
- Harness-side gates before composition: per-gateway `max_inflight` (§3.4) and `orchestration.max_fanout` (default 12). If a target gateway is at its limit, its sends queue — this IS the backpressure; there is no separate harness-side load probe beyond it (v1's host-load probe is subsumed; a gateway limit that reflects its host's capacity replaces a generic load average). - Scheduler-side authority: namespace `max_concurrent` and SlotPool caps apply regardless of what the harness requests (`FACT-10`, `FACT-16`); blackout windows still shift cost (`FACT-17`). The hierarchy is deliberately configured to *lose* to production lanes: director namespace weight low, `reserved=0`.

### 5.6 Fully-deferred fleet must idle, not burn
This is the invariant the 213-dry-run incident (`FACT-22`) demands:
- A cycle whose every send reports `deferred` (or whose supervisors report their foremen produced only `tasks_no_work`-class deferrals, `FACT-04`) closes as **drained**. A drained cycle schedules **no** follow-up wake, sends **no** chat messages, and the director's next cycle proceeds at its normal pin — it does not accelerate. - Hierarchy lanes are `admission_mode="cooldown"` with operator pins (`§3.2`): unlike the tasks lanes that caused the incident (`FACT-01`, `FACT-05`), a hierarchy lane with nothing to say re-admits only at its pin. `adaptive_cooldown` stays **on** for hierarchy lanes (it is only safe to disable where a workable-row gate exists — `FACT-05`) so repeated no-artifact hierarchy cycles also pace up. - The dry-run throttle (`warn 5 / suspend 10`, `FACT-06`) applies to hierarchy lanes too: ten consecutive cycles with no artifact and no directive that changed anything suspend the lane and page the owner. - **Normative R-013:** a hierarchy cycle that changes nothing must be cheaper than the cycle before it, bounded below by "no wake at all".

## 6. Security

### 6.1 Tool grants by role
Hermes sessions receive tool access via configuration; the per-session knob is SPIKE UQ-5. Grants are *config-defined per agent* in `harness.toml` and denied by default:
| Role | DuckBrain | Scheduler API | Shell / spawn | Fleet config (fleet.toml, scheduler.db) | |------|-----------|---------------|----------------|------------------------------------------| | supervisor | rw own rooms + own report messages | read-only (status, board) | none | none | | manager | rw own rooms + children's room reads | read-only | none | none | | manager↔manager (space) | rw the space rooms their registries justify | read-only | none | none | | director | rw own rooms + all room reads | read + **wake requests via harness**, never direct lane writes | none | none | | harness service | full `chd` ns | write: trigger registration + bump/wake requests, holding its own credential | n/a | writes only via loader/API path (`N-2`) | | **vp** (owner's agent surface — Hermes, Claude Code, MCP/API callers; RL-13) | read + post ONLY in rooms it names, via the harness ingress | none | none | none |
The VP is a first-class caller role (CT-10), not a hierarchy role: it chats into rooms just like a manager does, with exactly three grants — create objectives, inject messages, read rooms it names. **Harness-internal agents can NOT act as VP unless explicitly granted** — default-deny; a grant is one operator-written config flag per agent, and §6.3's write-gate rejects any agent-supplied request for it.
Agents never receive the scheduler's write credential, worker-spawn commands, or fleet.toml access. A supervisor therefore cannot dispatch workers (`FACT-23`'s `hermes chat` path is not in its grants) and cannot re-run foreman ticks.

### 6.2 Read-scoping enforcement point (survived from v1, room wording)
Two layers, one primary:
1. **Primary — the chat router (CT-07) at wake time.** The router is the only resolver of room membership; a session is *told* its own rooms and never learns the key names of rooms it does not belong to. An agent that cannot name a key cannot request it. 2. **Backstop — DuckBrain token scoping (UQ-2).** If DuckBrain can issue namespace-scoped tokens (`FACT-20` shows per-role token files exist), each agent's token confines it to its own namespace even against a colluding session. If UQ-2 falsifies scoping, this layer is documented as absent and layer 1 carries the guarantee alone — recorded as a known limitation, not hidden.

### 6.3 What prevents a supervisor from minting managers
Minting a manager = creating a scheduler lane, a harness agent entry, a DuckBrain identity, or a registry entry. Blocked at each path:
- **Lane creation is a scheduler mutation**, and every mutation passes the fail-closed auth gate — with auth off, mutations are refused 503 before any handler runs (`internal/api/auth_gate.go:9-13`, `FACT-15`). Only the harness service holds a mutating credential (§6.1). - **Agent config lives in `harness.toml`, operator-owned**, not in any DuckBrain key an agent can write; the harness loads it at startup and does not accept agent-written config keys (they are not in the CT-05 write families). - **DuckBrain identities are tokens on disk** (`FACT-20`), provisioned by the operator per agent; a supervisor's token confers no ability to mint another token (SPIKE: token-minting API surface — if DuckBrain exposes one, it is operator-gated and outside every agent grant). - **Registry entries are harness-written** (CT-09): an agent cannot grant itself a responsibility, and a manager-to-manager space without registry justification is refused by the router (§4.4). - **Precedent:** the fleet already gates "config that looks schedulable but drives something retired" at two pinned write paths (`FACT-09`). The same pattern is required for the harness: any agent-supplied string that would name a lane, model, room, or responsibility must be rejected at the harness's own write gate (M4 acceptance).

## 9. Multi-host deployment topology
**Requirement (owner directive):** the config knows which manager or supervisor lives on which host. The harness orchestrates a network of many Hermes systems, not one machine — managers and supervisors may sit on separate hosts (or separate profiles on one host), reached over Tailscale, reverse SSH tunnels, LAN port rules, or loopback. The full section lives in `sections/9-multi-host.top.md` and is summarized here; it is a first-class requirement, not an afterthought.
- **A host is anything running one addressable Hermes gateway** — another machine, another profile on this machine, or this machine (loopback). All three are the same thing to the config. - **Each agent row gains endpoint fields**: `gateway` (the Hermes URL that runs it), `transport` (`tailscale | ssh-tunnel | direct | loopback`), `auth_token_ref`. Role, grants, report key, wake triggers and channels are unchanged — the director/manager/supervisor contract is identical on every host; only the config gains the endpoint. - **The harness is the only cross-host hop.** A manager on host B reaching its supervisor on host C hands the message to the harness, which wakes C's supervisor. Read-scoping (§4.2) and the report contract (§4.6) are therefore enforced at ONE point, and no supervisor ever holds another host's credentials. - **Partitions are a report shape, not an error state**: an unreachable host yields MISSING reports (a visible absence — the dead-man rule), its wake rows pause as `paused:unreachable` instead of burning the re-prompt ladder against a dead socket, and the first healthy gateway check restores them. - **Transports never fail over silently**: a config that says `tailscale` fails loudly when the tailnet is down; it does not leak to a LAN route. - **Scale**: one harness, dozens of gateways; host count is bounded by the owner's network, not by the design.

## 11. Callers, Signal Surfaces, and the Crier Bridge

### 11.1 The VP caller role (RL-13, CT-10)
The owner's own agent surface talks to the director as the **VP** — a first-class caller role, peer to the hierarchy roles but outside the org chart:
- **Who is a VP.** Hermes (which has a TOOL to call the director), Claude Code, anything that speaks MCP or calls the harness API correctly. A VP sends messages to the director and chats just like a manager does. - **Grants, exactly three.** A VP may (1) create objectives (open rooms), (2) inject messages into rooms, (3) read rooms it names. The room names a VP may touch are config data (`vp.grants.rooms` in the contracts schema), never discovered. - **Default-deny inside the harness.** The director-harness's OWN agents — managers, supervisors, the director's sessions — can NOT act as VP unless explicitly granted (§6.1 table, §6.3 write gate). A hierarchy session presenting VP signals without the grant is a §6 integrity violation. - **Audit.** Every VP signal gets the same audit record (ingress log, CT-14) whichever door it used; a VP message into a room is a room message like any other — `from: vp/<surface-id>`, searchable (RL-15).

### 11.2 Signal surfaces — one contract, four doors (RL-16, CT-14)
The harness drives Hermes harnesses via SIGNALS. The ingress is ONE contract surface with four doors; the caller classes are VPs (other agents), the scheduler acting as VP, and a UI chat for the user:
| Door | Shape | Typical callers | |------|-------|-----------------| | **API** | HTTP POST to the harness ingress endpoint (the same endpoint a trigger lane's `gateway_url` names, `FACT-27`) | VPs (other agents); the scheduler acting as VP on tick fire (CT-02) | | **MCP** | the director exposed as MCP tools (e.g. the Hermes tool that calls the director) | VPs — Hermes, Claude Code, any MCP-speaking surface | | **CLI** | the harness CLI command (scripting, operator console) | the owner/operator; cron scripts | | **webhook** | inbound HTTP webhook from external systems | external automations granted VP |
Whatever enters any door is the SAME VP-signed signal: same authentication, same grants check (§11.1), same room-write rules, same audit record. No door is privileged; a caller's authority comes from its VP grant, never from which door it picked.

### 11.3 UI chat (RL-17)
A UI chat so the owner can follow along and watch the hierarchy work:
- **Read-only follower view by default.** The owner sees the rooms — every message, thread, and report — rendered from the DuckBrain logs (RL-15: the UI adds no store of its own, it reads `chd/*` keys). - **Posting = acting as VP.** The send box is a VP grant, not a bystander feature: a message posted through the UI enters through the harness ingress (§11.2) with the same VP grants, the same audit record, and the same no-self-echo rule (§4.4) as any other VP signal. - **Watching must never cost.** The follower view is pure read; it wakes no agent, consumes no session, and appears in no send_log.

### 11.4 Crier bridge (RL-18, CT-15, FACT-32)
The fleet already runs a crier Go bus for agent messages (`~/crier/README.md`, read 2026-11-07 — `FACT-32`). Its relevant surfaces, as the README documents them: a **relay** pub/sub where agents publish events to topics over HTTP/WS (`POST /relay/publish`, fire-and-forget, events delivered to subscribers exactly as published — `{"topic":"<published topic>","event":<event>}` — and DROPPED when a topic has zero subscribers); durable **per-agent inboxes** with lease-based delivery, ACK, TTL, idempotency keys, long-poll (`GET /agents/{id}/inbox?wait_seconds=N`) and a mesh `INBOX_NOTIFY` wake frame; per-agent **webhook delivery** (`PATCH /agents/{id}` with a `webhook` config); and bus-to-bus **federation**.
The bridge is an adapter the harness may configure per room — bridge support, not a dependency:
- **Outbound (director → crier).** A room configured `bridge: crier` has its events forwarded by the bridge: published to a crier topic (topic naming per config, e.g. `chd/room/<room-id>`) when subscribers are live, or delivered into a crier agent's durable inbox when the receiver must not lose the event — the README is explicit that a relay publish to an empty topic is dropped by design, so durable inbox delivery is the default for anything that matters. - **Inbound (crier → director).** The bridge long-polls a configured crier inbox; each retrieved (leased, ACKed) message becomes a room message `from: crier/<agent-id>` posted through the harness ingress (§11.2) — the same auth, grants check, and audit as any VP signal. - **Failure containment.** No hierarchy contract reads or writes crier: the verify loop, the ladder, and the caps (CT-06, §5.1, CT-13) run entirely on DuckBrain state (RL-15). A crier outage degrades the bridge only — rooms keep their own durable log, and undeliverable bridge traffic is dropped loudly (counted), never silently: a relay publish the bridge cannot confirm counts as a failed bridge delivery, mirroring crier's own `WEBHOOK_FAILED`-style error-notification shape.
